conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be part of your care team. You were admitted because of fever and worsening diarrhea. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had more frequent and watery output from my stoma, and I’ve felt weak. I had a low-grade fever at home too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your history. You’ve had a stem cell transplant recently and have a colostomy. We’re concerned this could be graft-versus-host disease, or GVHD, affecting your gut.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: GVHD again? I thought that was under control. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can happen after transplant. We’re taking it seriously. We’ll start you on IV steroids to calm the inflammation. We also need to rule out infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will I be on IV fluids too? I feel dehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve already started IV fluids. We’re also checking your labs and will do a CT scan to look at your intestines.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures and stool tests didn’t show any bacterial or viral infections. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection? What is it then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s GVHD. A biopsy confirmed inflammation in your gut from your donor immune cells attacking your tissues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. So the steroids will help with that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ve started IV methylprednisolone at 50 mg daily. We’ll monitor your response and adjust as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your CMV test back. Your viral load is low but detectable. This is common with immunosuppression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: CMV? I’ve had that before. Do I need treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re starting ganciclovir to prevent it from worsening. It’s given every 12 hours through your IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that make me feel worse? I’m already so tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can cause fatigue, but we’ll monitor your blood counts closely. The benefit outweighs the risk right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting TPN today because you’re not absorbing enough nutrition through your gut.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: TPN? Is that like IV nutrition?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it delivers nutrients directly into your bloodstream. It helps your gut rest and heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CMV viral load improved—from 370 to 190. That’s a good sign the ganciclovir is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Does that mean I can stop the IV medicine soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We’ll keep it going and recheck in a few days. We want to make sure it drops further.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stoma looks a bit inflamed. We’re adding metronidazole just in case there’s a bacterial component.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it infected? Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of infection. It might be related to GVHD or irritation. We’ll watch it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a CT scan today for new abdominal pain. Good news—no appendicitis or obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But there was something on the scan, right? You looked concerned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw some new lung opacities. We’re following up with a chest CT to check for pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The chest CT shows patchy opacities in your lower lungs. It looks like pneumonia, likely from a virus or mild infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pneumonia? But I’m not coughing much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some patients don’t have classic symptoms, especially with weakened immunity. We’re starting cefepime and azithromycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need oxygen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not now. Your oxygen levels are good. We’ll monitor closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stool output has improved—from 650 cc to 300 cc daily—and it’s thicker. That means your gut is healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Can I start eating again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re advancing you to Phase V of the GI GVHD diet—soft, low-residue foods. We’ll go slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you IV immunoglobulin today. Your IgG levels were low, so this helps boost your immunity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I used to get that every few weeks. I’ve missed a few doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll resume regular IVIG after discharge. It’s important for preventing infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CMV viral load is now undetectable. We’ll switch you to oral valganciclovir before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can stop the IV medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll transition to a once-daily pill. You’ll take it at home for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sputum culture showed some staph, but it’s not resistant. It’s likely just colonizing, not causing infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be on antibiotics for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we don’t think it’s causing harm. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver enzymes were a bit high, but they’re improving. Likely due to medications, not serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Which meds are affecting my liver?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tacrolimus and voriconazole can. We’re watching levels and adjusting doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been off TPN for two days and eating well. That’s a big step forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m actually hungry! That feels good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad. We’ll keep you on the soft diet and monitor your stoma output.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your leg swelling was checked with an ultrasound. No blood clot—good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was worried about that. What’s causing the swelling then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely fluid overload from IV fluids and TPN. It should improve now that we’ve stopped them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. You’ve made great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. What meds will I go home on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue prednisone, tacrolimus, budesonide, and now valganciclovir. We’re adjusting insulin too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood sugar has been high. Will the new doses help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re increasing your long-acting insulin and restarting metformin. We’ll follow closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my back pain? It’s been worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve adjusted your methadone and will refer you back to pain clinic. We know it’s been tough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re doing well—clear lungs, stable vitals, and good oral intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so grateful. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Watch for fever, increased diarrhea, or shortness of breath. Call us if any of those happen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up appointments?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your transplant, oncology, and GI teams. We’ll send all the details.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard. Keep taking your meds and eating well. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Dr. Lee.
